items.title: Defence: the self-reliance decade
items.summary: Why we treat India’s defence manufacturing as a multi-year order book, not a theme — and how we decide which companies have earned a place.
items.body:
For most of the last fifty years, India bought its defence equipment abroad. That is changing, and not because of a single budget or a single announcement. Procurement rules now favour domestic manufacturers, export ambitions have become explicit, and a generation of Indian companies has spent the last decade building the capability to deliver.

We do not buy a theme. A sector can be right for a decade and still be the wrong place to pay any price. What we look for is visibility: order books that stretch years ahead, execution records that show contracts turning into revenue on time, and balance sheets strong enough to fund the working capital that defence contracts demand.

The risks are real — lumpy orders, government as the dominant customer, and valuations that can run well ahead of earnings. That is why sizing matters as much as selection. Where defence appears in a client portfolio, it is sized to the family’s horizon and risk appetite, not to the enthusiasm of the market.

The question we keep asking is simple: if the share price did nothing for three years, would we be comfortable owning this business? Only those that pass make it into the portfolios we manage.

items.title: Power equipment and the grid India now has to build
items.summary: Electricity demand, renewables and data centres are forcing a once-in-a-generation build-out of transmission and equipment. Here is how we think about owning it.
items.body:
Every new factory, metro line, data centre and solar park needs one thing first: power that reaches it reliably. India’s demand for electricity is rising, and the grid that carries it — transformers, switchgear, cables, transmission lines — has to grow faster than it has in decades.

This is what makes power equipment interesting to us. It is not a bet on any one fuel. Whether the next unit of electricity comes from coal, sun or wind, it still has to be transmitted, stepped down and distributed. The companies that make that equipment sit underneath the entire energy transition.

Capital-goods cycles are long, and they reward patience more than timing. We prefer manufacturers with pricing power, healthy order inflows and the discipline not to chase low-margin contracts for the sake of growth. We are equally careful about what has already been priced in.

In practice, power equipment sits alongside other domestic manufacturing in the portfolios where it fits — never as a concentrated wager, always as part of a plan built around a family’s goals.

items.title: Gold and silver in a bespoke portfolio
items.summary: Precious metals are not a trade for us. They are ballast — and how much ballast each family needs is a personal decision, not a market call.
items.body:
Gold has done what it has always done in uncertain years: held its value when other assets wobbled. Silver, more industrial and more volatile, tends to amplify those moves in both directions. Neither pays a dividend, and neither should be expected to compound like a good business.

So why hold them at all? Because a portfolio is not judged only by how fast it grows, but by whether a family can stay invested through difficult markets. A measured allocation to precious metals can steady the whole, especially when currencies or interest rates move sharply.

How much is right depends entirely on the family. A business owner with a concentrated exposure to one industry may need more ballast than a salaried professional with steady income. This is where bespoke portfolios matter — no two of the portfolios we manage carry the same mix, because no two families face the same risks.

We access precious metals through efficient, regulated instruments such as ETFs and funds rather than physical holdings, and we review the allocation alongside everything else, every quarter.
